editorial:
The Son of Tarzan is a silent fifteen-part serial released in 1920, adapted from Edgar Rice Burroughs' 1915 novel of the same name. The Internet Archive's description says the scenario follows the book closely. The picture is a cliffhanger serial, so it suits reuse as episodic archival footage, a jungle-adventure sample, or a silent-era study.

The film's release in 1920 puts it past US copyright term, and the source novel, serialized in All-Story Weekly in 1915 and 1916, is also past term. The rights trap is not the film or the story. It is anything added to a particular copy: a modern score, new intertitles, or a restoration's added material. Character and franchise trademarks tied to Tarzan are a separate question that this dossier has not resolved.
faq: Can I reuse footage from the 1920 serial?

The 1920 film print and the underlying novel are past US copyright term, so the images can be reused in the US. Check the particular copy for added music, new titles or other additions, which can carry their own rights.
Does the Tarzan trademark still matter?

Possibly. Trademarks on the character or franchise can outlast copyright, and this dossier has not confirmed whether any is active. Avoid using Tarzan branding in a way that suggests an official product.
